ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 14.0 / Reykjanes → Reykjavík / ⚓ Hafnir
en: A Ship With Nobody Aboard, And A Hall That Is Too Old

ctx: opening hook line — tour 14.0 / Reykjanes → Reykjavík / ⚓ Hafnir
en: Two things happened in this village that should not have. A **ship with no crew** delivered Iceland's biggest timber windfall of the century. And archaeologists dug up a **hall that appears to be older than the settlement of Iceland is supposed to be.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Reykjanes → Reykjavík / ⚓ Hafnir
en: Start with the hall. In **November 2002** the archaeologist **Bjarni F. Einarsson** was looking at an aerial photograph and spotted the outline of a longhouse in the field **behind Kirkjuvogskirkja.** They dug two holes. The second hit the **long-hearth** just under a metre down. Charcoal from that hearth went for radiocarbon dating.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Reykjanes → Reykjavík / ⚓ Hafnir
en: Say the result carefully, because it matters. The site's own museum — **Byggðasafn Reykjanesbæjar** — describes it as a **ninth-century hall, probably built before the date conventionally given for the settlement of Iceland, and in use into the tenth century.** The information board on site says only *"strong indication that the farm was built before the year 900."* That is the claim. It has not been overturned and it has not been formally endorsed. **Do not let anyone tell you it rewrites the textbooks — the excavators themselves have not said that.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Reykjanes → Reykjavík / ⚓ Hafnir
en: The building was about **17 metres long and 7 wide**, with two sunken structures beside it, and a geophysical survey suggested **five more buildings** around it. It has been re-turfed, with the hearth marked out in lava slabs, so you can walk the outline.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Reykjanes → Reykjavík / ⚓ Hafnir
en: Now the ship. In **June 1881** a huge American vessel came ashore here — **three masts, three decks, about 110 metres long** — **completely empty of people.** She had been abandoned in the Atlantic months earlier, her crew taken off by a steamer, and she had drifted for something like **four months** with seventeen feet of water in her. When Icelanders reached the deck there was **grass growing on it.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Reykjanes → Reykjavík / ⚓ Hafnir
en: She was the **Jamestown**, fully loaded with **finished hardwood** bound for England. On the date, the sources fight: the **US Navy report says 26 June.** The **Icelandic eyewitness** — Ólafur Ketilsson, who was **sixteen and standing on the wreck**, writing it up in 1930 — says **Whit Sunday morning**, which was **5 June.** They cannot both be right and I am not going to smooth it over for you.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Reykjanes → Reykjavík / ⚓ Hafnir
en: The locals **refused the salvage job.** Three Reykjavík men took it on, hired crews at **25 aurar an hour**, and — this detail is from the boy who was there — paid them **in gold and silver, every Saturday evening.** The timber went into houses right across Suðurnes and inland. **Þorvarðarhús**, the oldest house in Keflavík, is clad in it. A luthier has since built violins and cellos using Jamestown wood for the soundposts.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Reykjanes → Reykjavík / ⚓ Hafnir
en: One of the ship's **anchors stands beside Kirkjuvogskirkja** in this village. The other is at Sáðgerði in Sandgerði.

ctx: the point of the block — tour 14.0 / Reykjanes → Reykjavík / ✈️ Keflavík
en: A wartime airstrip became a Cold War base, became a shopping-and-housing district, became the busiest transatlantic stopover in the North Atlantic. Same tarmac. Four completely different countries' worth of history.

ctx: the spoken close — tour 14.0 / Reykjanes → Reykjavík / ✈️ Keflavík

ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 14.0 / Reykjanes → Reykjavík / ✈️ Keflavík
en: The Airport You Arrived At, And The Base That Built It

ctx: opening hook line — tour 14.0 / Reykjanes → Reykjavík / ✈️ Keflavík
en: Almost everyone on this bus landed there. It was built by the **US military in the Second World War**, it was an **American base for fifty-five years**, and the Americans went home on **30 September 2006.** The airport you walked through is the leftovers.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Reykjanes → Reykjavík / ✈️ Keflavík
en: There were originally **two** airfields. **Patterson Field** was started in **February 1942** up by Fitjar. **Meeks Field** — which is the one still here — was begun that summer on Háaleiti by a US Navy construction battalion, with about **3,000 men** working on it at the peak. It opened in **1943.** *(Sources give three different days in March and April 1943 for the ceremony, so I will give you the year and keep my dignity.)*

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Reykjanes → Reykjavík / ✈️ Keflavík
en: Both were named after **young American pilots killed in Iceland.** Meeks died in a crash at Reykjavík airport on **19 August 1941**, shortly after arriving in the country. The busiest month was **June 1944**: **1,050 aircraft** through the field, and on one day, **115 four-engine bombers** on the ground at once.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Reykjanes → Reykjavík / ✈️ Keflavík
en: The airfields became Icelandic property under the **1946 agreement** and the last wartime US troops left on **8 April 1947.** Then the Cold War arrived: the **defence agreement was signed on 5 May 1951**, and the base ran for the next fifty-five years. On **1 March 1990** there were **3,294 US military personnel** here — **4,987** counting families — plus **1,086 Icelandic employees.** By January **2005** the military figure was down to **1,453.** On **15 March 2006** Washington gave notice, and on **30 September 2006** they were gone.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Reykjanes → Reykjavík / ✈️ Keflavík
en: What happens when a foreign army hands you a town? Iceland set up a development company on **24 October 2006** and turned the base into **Ásbrú** — housing, businesses and a campus. *(The university side has just changed hands again: teaching stayed on Ásbrú but the **University of Iceland took it over on 1 January 2026.**)*

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Reykjanes → Reykjavík / ✈️ Keflavík
en: The airport itself became the country's front door. The **Leifur Eiríksson terminal** opened on **14 April 1987** at **23,000 square metres.** In **2025** it handled **8,159,461 passengers** — the fourth-busiest year in its history. **2.2 million** of those, **27%**, never left the building — they were changing planes between America and Europe, which is the entire business model of this country's aviation.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Reykjanes → Reykjavík / ✈️ Keflavík
en: And the town is **Reykjanesbær**, created on **11 June 1994** by merging **Keflavík, Njarðvík and Hafnir** — **10,181 people** at the time.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Reykjanes → Reykjavík / ✈️ Keflavík
en: One story for the road. On **9 October 1986**, Air Force One landed here at **five past seven in the evening** carrying **Ronald Reagan**, for the summit with **Gorbachev** in Reykjavík. The talks collapsed. On the **12th**, before flying home, Reagan stopped at this base to speak to the American personnel and explained why he was late: *"I called Nancy and told her I wouldn't be home for dinner."*

en: 🪦 Vogastapi

ctx: cue, tells the guest where to look — tour 14.0 / Reykjanes → Reykjavík / 🪦 Vogastapi
en: Look left — the long flat-topped headland dropping into the sea.

ctx: the point of the block — tour 14.0 / Reykjanes → Reykjavík / 🪦 Vogastapi
en: A headland with three recorded deaths from exposure, a fourth party who went over the cliff, and a ghost tradition that is really just an unlit road with a drop on one side and no reliable directions.

ctx: the spoken close — tour 14.0 / Reykjanes → Reykjavík / 🪦 Vogastapi
en: They spent thirty-eight years arguing about doubling this road. The ghost outlasted the debate. Then in December they finished it — and by the best available folklore, that was his notice period.

ctx: bad-weather alternative — tour 14.0 / Reykjanes → Reykjavík / 🪦 Vogastapi
en: Weather pivot (ideal here): "This is the weather that killed people on this headland. On a clear day the ghost story sounds silly. Today it does not."

ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 14.0 / Reykjanes → Reykjavík / 🪦 Vogastapi
en: The Ghost That May Have Been Made Redundant Last December

ctx: opening hook line — tour 14.0 / Reykjanes → Reykjavík / 🪦 Vogastapi
en: In **1990** the folklorist **Árni Björnsson** wrote that the ghost of this headland had gone quiet since the new road was built, and predicted he would **vanish altogether once the road was finally doubled.** That doubling was completed on **11 December 2025.** So either he has retired, or he is extremely annoyed.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Reykjanes → Reykjavík / 🪦 Vogastapi
en: **Vogastapi** is about **80 metres** high, older grey basalt sitting between the young lavas either side of it. Its high point is **Grímshóll**, and there is a view-disc up there. The municipality's own website states, without hedging, that **the Stapi is haunted.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Reykjanes → Reykjavík / 🪦 Vogastapi
en: The University of Iceland's science service is refreshingly deflating about the ghost. **Stapadraugurinn** — the Stapi ghost — has **no origin story at all.** Nobody recorded who he was or how he got there. All that survives is that he roughed travellers up. The one documented case is from the **1870s**: a man from Garður was found half-dead on the headland, carried to the farm at Stapakot, and **never once explained what had happened to him.** They blamed the ghost.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Reykjanes → Reykjavík / 🪦 Vogastapi
en: The better-attested haunting has a reason. A traveller asked for lodging in **Vogar** and was **turned away.** He set off over the Stapi in bad weather and was **found dead by Grímshóll the next morning.** They carried his body back to the very farm that had refused him, and buried him. The haunting started immediately after. *(There is a moral in there and it is not subtle.)*

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Reykjanes → Reykjavík / 🪦 Vogastapi
en: The modern version is a **phantom hitchhiker.** He stands at the roadside, gets in when someone kindly stops, will not say where he is going, says nothing at all — and after a while is simply not there.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Reykjanes → Reykjavík / 🪦 Vogastapi
en: And here is why the ghost stories are so thick on this one headland: **people kept dying on it.** **28 January 1859** — Þorsteinn from Stapakot, lost in the open. Around **1865** — a fish-buyer named Egill and his companions took the wrong path in a blizzard and **went over the cliffs.** Their bodies were found broken at the bottom. Around **1870** — Sveinbjörn from Stapakot, exposure again. Árni Óla wrote the plain explanation in **1961**: *because so many died on the Stapi, it was long thought deeply haunted.*

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Reykjanes → Reykjavík / 🪦 Vogastapi
en: The road is the sequel. This stretch became **Iceland's first concrete road** in the national network in **October 1965**, with **tolls charged until 1972.** Alþingi was asked to double it **six times between 1987 and 1992.** The last 5.6-kilometre section finally opened on **11 December 2025.** It now carries about **21,500 vehicles a day.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Reykjanes → Reykjavík / 🪦 Vogastapi
en: The village below is **Vogar** — **2,005 people** as of **1 August 2026**, up from **1,308** in 2019. **The fastest-growing municipality on this peninsula**, in the decade the peninsula started erupting again.

ctx: the point of the block — tour 14.0 / Reykjanes → Reykjavík / 🔺 Keilir

ctx: the spoken close — tour 14.0 / Reykjanes → Reykjavík / 🔺 Keilir
en: The most volcano-looking volcano in Iceland is the one that is definitely never going to erupt. Everything on this peninsula that looks safe is not, and everything that looks dangerous is retired. Welcome to Reykjanes.

en: Weather pivot: "Keilir is the first thing to disappear and the first thing to come back. If you cannot see it, the locals cannot either, and they have been complaining about that for a thousand years."

ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 14.0 / Reykjanes → Reykjavík / 🔺 Keilir
en: The Cone That Only Ever Erupted Once

ctx: opening hook line — tour 14.0 / Reykjanes → Reykjavík / 🔺 Keilir
en: It looks exactly like a child's drawing of a volcano, so here is the twist: **it is not one.** Not the kind you are thinking of. It erupted **once**, under a glacier, and **it will never erupt again.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Reykjanes → Reykjavík / 🔺 Keilir
en: **Keilir** is **379 metres** above sea level — but only about **200 metres above the ground at its foot**, which is the number to have ready when a guest checks their phone and looks at you funny. Both are true.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Reykjanes → Reykjavík / 🔺 Keilir
en: It is a **móbergsfell** — a hyaloclastite cone. It formed in a **single eruption beneath the ice sheet of the last glacial period.** These volcanoes erupt **once in their lifetime** and then they are finished. The University of Iceland's own science service puts it flatly: *Keilir is a hyaloclastite cone and it will not erupt again.*

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Reykjanes → Reykjavík / 🔺 Keilir
en: The cone shape has a cause. The little cap on the summit is almost certainly the **plugged conduit** — the last of the magma, frozen solid in the pipe at the end of the eruption. The soft ash around it wore away. The hard plug did not. **You are looking at a volcano that has been eroded down to its own spine.** And nobody knows its age — it has never been dated.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Reykjanes → Reykjavík / 🔺 Keilir
en: Icelandic field researchers record it as a **mið**, a navigation transit: seamen lined up on Keilir to find their way in, for example running into **Hamarssund** on the approach to **Sandgerði.** A mountain used as a landmark by people who had no charts and no lights.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Reykjanes → Reykjavík / 🔺 Keilir
en: And it had a starring role in the modern eruptions, which is usually told wrong. In **March 2021**, a **dyke** — a blade of magma — pushed up along a line running **from Keilir south to Fagradalsfjall.** Thousands of earthquakes tracked it moving. It finally broke the surface at the **southern end** of that line, in **Geldingadalur**, on **19 March 2021 at about a quarter to nine in the evening.** So: the **magma** ran between Keilir and Fagradalsfjall. The **eruption** was at the far end of it, where we were standing this morning.

ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 14.0 / Reykjanes → Reykjavík / 🌑 Route 41
en: The Moon Road

ctx: opening hook line — tour 14.0 / Reykjanes → Reykjavík / 🌑 Route 41
en: NASA sent thirty-two astronauts to Iceland to learn how to read rock — Armstrong among them. This is the rock.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Reykjanes → Reykjavík / 🌑 Route 41
en: The lava out both windows looked so alien that **NASA used Iceland as an astronaut training ground.** During the **Apollo programme (1965–67)**, **32 astronauts** — **Neil Armstrong** among them — trained on Icelandic rock. The heavy fieldwork was at **Askja** in the highlands, but the Reykjanes flows you are passing are the same **young basalt.** Volcanologist **Sigurður Þórarinsson** guided the crews.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Reykjanes → Reykjavík / 🌑 Route 41
en: The two lava types here — **pahoehoe** (smooth, ropy) and **aa** (rough, jagged) — are the same textures mapped on the Moon and Mars. In **2023** the **NASA Artemis** astronauts came back to the same fields to train for humanity's return to the Moon.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Reykjanes → Reykjavík / 🌑 Route 41
en: Reading the age of it is easy once you know the trick: **nothing grows on it.** The jet-black, plant-free fields are the new ones. The older flows toward Hafnarfjörður are ~**700 to 1,000 years old** — medieval — and still look like last week's, because Iceland has almost **no weathering**: no acid rain, no baking heat, no forest to break the rock down. *(Nothing tidies up here. It just sits there looking new for a thousand years, like a show home.)*

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Reykjanes → Reykjavík / 🌑 Route 41
en: And a fair bit of it is hollow. **Lava tubes** form where the surface crusts over while molten rock keeps running underneath, then drains away and leaves the pipe behind. The pile is hundreds of metres thick, but the tubes sit just under the crust — sometimes **only a metre or two below the wheels.** *(You are, in a modest way, driving on a ceiling.)*

ctx: opening hook line — tour 14.0 / Reykjanes → Reykjavík / 🏙️ Reykjavík
en: The northernmost capital on Earth. Named for smoke that turned out to be steam. Heated by a hot spring that has never once posted an oil bill.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Reykjanes → Reykjavík / 🏙️ Reykjavík
en: ***Reykjavík* = "Smoky Bay."** Around **874 AD** the chieftain **Ingólfur Arnarson** sailed in, saw steam off the geothermal vents, and called it smoke. It wasn't — those **hot springs** now heat nearly every building in the city.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Reykjanes → Reykjavík / 🏙️ Reykjavík
en: Archaeology backs the legend: a turf longhouse wall at **Aðalstræti** lies **under a volcanic ash layer dated to AD 871 ±2** — the founding pinned to within two years by Greenland ice cores. It is on show *in situ* at the **Settlement Exhibition.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Reykjanes → Reykjavík / 🏙️ Reykjavík
en: It is the world's **northernmost capital** at **64°N.** **Two-thirds of all Icelanders** — roughly **250,000 of 394,324** (Hagstofa Íslands, 1 January 2026) — live in the greater city, almost entirely on **geothermal heat**: **80–90°C** water piped to radiators, pools and snow-free pavements. Reykjavík was the **first major city to quit oil heating**, done by the **1970s.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Reykjanes → Reykjavík / 🏙️ Reykjavík
en: Which closes the loop on the whole day. **Everything you have looked at today — Seltún, Svartsengi, Gunnuhver, the plant at Reykjanes — is the same heat that warms the shower in your hotel tonight.** The peninsula that keeps trying to erupt is also the reason this country stopped burning oil.
